"You're right, boy," I told Bruiser as we walked down the rocky beach together. "Sometimes I wish those mornings—drawing men home across open water—never happened." He looked up at me with understanding eyes, his ears perked slightly forward. That morning had been different. Different from all the others. The sea had been calm, almost mirror-like, reflecting the sky perfectly. He probably didn't understand exactly why it mattered—that day still haunted me when I closed my eyes—but he sensed change in people easier than anyone I'd ever known. We reached the small pile of stones near our favorite spot—a granite outcropping where we'd watch sunsets when I still went out fishing regularly. I picked up a handful of pebbles, examining each one carefully before adding it to the growing monument to our years together. Each stone represented a day we'd stood here as companions—the calm before storms, the triumph after successful returns, and yes, sometimes those days like today where memories yield bitter regrets. I placed another stone beside the others, this onecarefully selected for its smooth texture, then sat down beside Bruiser. He positioned himself closer than usual, nuzzling gently against my thigh. "I remember when you were just a pup," I whispered. "Your energy was boundless—you'd bark at every wave crashing against the shore."
